title: dbConnect() leaks the SQLite handle when the database fails to open
description:
## Summary

When `sqlite3_open_v2()` fails, for example because the file's directory does
not exist, `DbConnection::DbConnection()` raises an error without closing the
handle SQLite returned. The handle and its allocations are lost, about 750–850
bytes on each failed `dbConnect()`. valgrind reports them as "definitely
lost", so CRAN's valgrind check shows the leak against any package whose tests
exercise a failing connection.

## Setup

This is a stock Ubuntu 24.04 with distribution packages and CRAN's packages
built from source. No special R build is needed.

| Component | Version | Installed with |
|---|---|---|
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, x86_64 | `ubuntu:24.04` container |
| R | 4.3.3 | `apt-get install r-base-dev` |
| C/C++ compiler | gcc 13.3.0 | comes with `r-base-dev` |
| valgrind | 3.22.0 | `apt-get install valgrind` |
| DBI | 1.3.0 | `install.packages("DBI")` from CRAN |
| RSQLite | 3.53.3 (bundled SQLite 3.53.3) | `install.packages("RSQLite")` from CRAN, built from source |

From scratch:

```sh
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends r-base-dev valgrind ca-certificates
Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("DBI", "RSQLite"), repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")'
```

The same leak also shows on R-devel (r90742) built with clang 23 and libc++
on Fedora 44 with valgrind 3.27.1, and in R-hub's valgrind image
(`ghcr.io/r-hub/containers/valgrind`). It doesn't depend on the compiler or
the C++ standard library.

## Reproducible example

`leak.R`:

```r
n <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("N", "1"))
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  try(DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "/nonexistent/dir/db.sqlite"), silent = TRUE)
}
```

`control.R`, a connection that opens and is closed:

```r
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

Run:

```sh
N=1  R -d "valgrind --leak-check=full" --vanilla -q -f leak.R
N=10 R -d "valgrind --leak-check=full" --vanilla -q -f leak.R
R -d "valgrind --leak-check=full" --vanilla -q -f control.R
```

`definitely lost` in valgrind's LEAK SUMMARY:

| Run | RSQLite 3.53.3 from CRAN | With the fix below |
|---|---|---|
| `leak.R`, 1 failed connection | 848 bytes in 2 blocks | 0 bytes |
| `leak.R`, 10 failed connections | 7,344 bytes in 12 blocks | 0 bytes |
| `control.R` | 0 bytes | — |

Stacks of the two lost blocks for `N=1`, taken from two runs of the same
setup. The first is the connection object allocated by `openDatabase()`; the
second is memory SQLite attached to it while opening. Addresses are removed,
the `std::string` template arguments are shortened to `std::string`, and the
deepest frames are cut:

```
==5051== 848 (800 direct, 48 indirect) bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 235 of 1,786
==5051==    at malloc (in /usr/libexec/valgrind/vgpreload_memcheck-amd64-linux.so)
==5051==    by sqlite3MemMalloc (sqlite3.c:28035)
==5051==    by mallocWithAlarm (sqlite3.c:31754)
==5051==    by sqlite3Malloc (sqlite3.c:31779)
==5051==    by sqlite3Malloc (sqlite3.c:31773)
==5051==    by sqlite3MallocZero (sqlite3.c:32058)
==5051==    by openDatabase (sqlite3.c:190784)
==5051==    by DbConnection::DbConnection(std::string const&, bool, int, std::string const&, bool) (DbConnection.cpp:15)
==5051==    by connection_connect(std::string const&, bool, int, std::string const&, bool) (connection.cpp:41)

==4208== 552 (48 direct, 504 indirect) bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 190 of 1,786
==4208==    at malloc (in /usr/libexec/valgrind/vgpreload_memcheck-amd64-linux.so)
==4208==    by sqlite3MemMalloc (sqlite3.c:28035)
==4208==    by mallocWithAlarm (sqlite3.c:31754)
==4208==    by sqlite3Malloc (sqlite3.c:31779)
==4208==    by sqlite3Malloc (sqlite3.c:31773)
==4208==    by sqlite3HashInsert (sqlite3.c:38907)
==4208==    by findCollSeqEntry (sqlite3.c:132474)
==4208==    by sqlite3FindCollSeq.part.0 (sqlite3.c:132516)
==4208==    by sqlite3FindCollSeq (sqlite3.c:132515)
```


The user sees the expected error in both versions:

```
Error : Could not connect to database:
unable to open database file
```

## Cause

`src/DbConnection.cpp`, unchanged on `main` (commit `b48403d`, 3.53.3.9020):

```cpp
  int rc = sqlite3_open_v2(
    path.c_str(),
    &pConn_,
    flags | SQLITE_OPEN_URI,
    vfs.empty() ? NULL : vfs.c_str()
  );
  if (rc != SQLITE_OK) {
    cpp11::stop("Could not connect to database:\n%s", getException().c_str());
  }
```

`sqlite3_open_v2()` usually allocates a handle even when it fails. SQLite's
documentation for it says: "Whether or not an error occurs when it is opened,
resources associated with the database connection handle should be released
by passing it to `sqlite3_close()` when it is no longer required."

`cpp11::stop()` throws from inside the constructor, so `~DbConnection()`
never runs and `disconnect()` is never called on the half-open handle.

## Fix

Tested on the setup above, giving the "with the fix" column. `getException()`
reads `sqlite3_errmsg(pConn_)`, so it must be called before the handle is
closed. The error message is unchanged:

```diff
--- a/src/DbConnection.cpp
+++ b/src/DbConnection.cpp
@@ -19,7 +19,10 @@
     vfs.empty() ? NULL : vfs.c_str()
   );
   if (rc != SQLITE_OK) {
-    cpp11::stop("Could not connect to database:\n%s", getException().c_str());
+    std::string msg = getException();
+    sqlite3_close_v2(pConn_);
+    pConn_ = NULL;
+    cpp11::stop("Could not connect to database:\n%s", msg.c_str());
   }
   if (allow_ext) {
     sqlite3_enable_load_extension(pConn_, 1);
```

`sqlite3_close_v2(NULL)` is a harmless no-op, which covers the rare case in
which SQLite cannot allocate a handle at all. RSQLite's own test suite has
not been run against the patch.

## How this came up

opentimsr's tests check that opening a folder without a database fails
cleanly. R-hub's valgrind check flagged this leak in that test.
opentimsr 1.2.3 now checks that the file exists before calling
`dbConnect()`. Other packages that test a failing connection will see the
same report.

title: NORET attribute is misplaced
Remove the deprecated pkgconfig setting for the `row.names` default
description:
RSQLite 2.0 changed the default of `row.names` to `FALSE` (#210) and offered `pkgconfig::set_config("RSQLite::row.names.query" = NA)` (and `"RSQLite::row.names.table"`) as a temporary, per-package way to restore the old default.

#805 deprecates this. The `row.names` arguments of `dbFetch()`, `dbReadTable()`, `dbWriteTable()`, `sqlData()`, and `sqliteBuildTableDefinition()` now default to a plain `FALSE`, and pkgconfig moved from Imports to Suggests. A value set via pkgconfig is still honored if pkgconfig is already loaded, with a warning once per session. The logic lives in `row_names_default()` in `R/pkgconfig.R`.

Once a release with the deprecation is on CRAN, remove the setting entirely:

- [ ] Search CRAN code for `RSQLite::row.names` to check that no package still relies on the setting.
- [ ] Remove the `if (missing(row.names)) row.names <- row_names_default(...)` blocks from the five functions above.
- [ ] Delete `R/pkgconfig.R` and its `Collate` entry in `DESCRIPTION`.
- [ ] Drop pkgconfig from Suggests.
- [ ] Reduce `tests/testthat/test-row-names-default.R` to the test that `row.names` defaults to `FALSE`.

Callers who still need the old behavior pass `row.names = NA` explicitly.

title: Using `[1]` instead of `[]` breaks the strict bounds checks.
description:
From CRAN:

We are seeing UBSAN errors in CRAN packages

CAESAR.Suite Cyclops GRIN2 LowWAFOMNX MOCHA Mega2R PAMmisc PANACEA
RecordLinkage SSN2 WGCNA bigsnpr dexter dexterMST epoxy glue idem
netgsa prqlr qtl2 rliger sf snplist storr stream survey taxonomizr winch

most at

vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.c:111455:20: runtime error: index 2 out of bounds for type 'ExprList_item [1]'
    #0 0x7f88b04dd803 in sqlite3ExprListAppend vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.c:111455

We have been here before: it is found by `-fsanitize=strict-bounds` in GCC.

This comes from

```c
struct ExprList {
  int nExpr;             /* Number of expressions on the list */
  int nAlloc;            /* Number of a[] slots allocated */
  struct ExprList_item { /* For each expression in the list */
    Expr *pExpr;            /* The parse tree for this expression */
    char *zEName;           /* Token associated with this expression */
    struct {
      u8 sortFlags;           /* Mask of KEYINFO_ORDER_* flags */
      unsigned eEName :2;     /* Meaning of zEName */
      unsigned done :1;       /* Indicates when processing is finished */
      unsigned reusable :1;   /* Constant expression is reusable */
      unsigned bSorterRef :1; /* Defer evaluation until after sorting */
      unsigned bNulls :1;     /* True if explicit "NULLS FIRST/LAST" */
      unsigned bUsed :1;      /* This column used in a SF_NestedFrom subquery */
      unsigned bUsingTerm:1;  /* Term from the USING clause of a NestedFrom */
      unsigned bNoExpand: 1;  /* Term is an auxiliary in NestedFrom and should
                              ** not be expanded by "*" in parent queries */
    } fg;
    union {
      struct {             /* Used by any ExprList other than Parse.pConsExpr */
        u16 iOrderByCol;      /* For ORDER BY, column number in result set */
        u16 iAlias;           /* Index into Parse.aAlias[] for zName */
      } x;
      int iConstExprReg;   /* Register in which Expr value is cached. Used only
                           ** by Parse.pConstExpr */
    } u;
  } a[1];                  /* One slot for each expression in the list */
};
```

That is pre-C99 code, and should be `a[]`.

similarly,

```
  u32 aType[1];           /* Type values record decode.  MUST BE LAST */
  CollSeq *aColl[1];  /* Collating sequence for each term of the key */
```

should be `[]`

Temporarily we have installed RSQLite without using strict-bounds.

Packages GRIN2 Mega2R ProFAST dexter dexterMST rliger

show another issue

vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.c:79337:14: runtime error: load of address 0x7f2fb0869240 with insufficient space for an object of type 'struct MemPage *'

at

balance_nonroot vendor/sqlite3/sqlite3.c:79337

Please investigate and if necessary report upstream.

title: bug: `http.c` fails to compile on GCC < C23 default
description:
The HTTP/HTTPS VFS added in #680 (and released in 3.53.2) defines functions with unnamed parameters in their definitions, for example:

```c
static int httpWrite(sqlite3_file*, const void*, int, sqlite3_int64){ return SQLITE_READONLY; }
```

Omitting parameter names in a function *definition* (not just a prototype) is only valid in **C23** and in C++. Toolchains that default to an older C dialect reject it with `error: parameter name omitted`. This breaks every build on RHEL8-like distros, whose system compiler is GCC 8.5 (`gnu17`).

## Reprex

On any RHEL8-family system running `R CMD BUILD`

```
vendor/extensions/http.c:108:22: error: parameter name omitted
 static int httpWrite(sqlite3_file*, const void*, int, sqlite3_int64){ return SQLITE_READONLY; }
                      ^~~~~~~~~~~~~
vendor/extensions/http.c:109:25: error: parameter name omitted
 static int httpTruncate(sqlite3_file*, sqlite3_int64){ return SQLITE_READONLY; }
...
make: *** [ext-http.o] Error 1
ERROR: compilation failed for package 'RSQLite'
```

Minimal standalone reprex:

```sh
printf 'static int f(int, int){ return 0; }\nint main(void){ return f(1,2); }\n' > t.c
gcc -std=gnu17 -c t.c     # error: parameter name omitted   (default on GCC 8.5)
gcc -std=gnu2x -c t.c     # OK
```

title: `dbFetch()` gives confusing warning when used with `dbSendStatement()`
description:
Calling `dbFetch()` on a result of `dbSendStatement()` gives a confusing warning, telling you to use `dbSendStatement()`:

``` r
library(DBI)

fetch_bound_statement <- function(drv) {
  con <- dbConnect(drv, ":memory:")  
  on.exit(dbDisconnect(con), add = TRUE)
  dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE foo (bar TEXT)")
  
  res <- dbSendStatement(con, "INSERT INTO foo (bar) VALUES (?)")
  on.exit(dbClearResult(res), add = TRUE, after = FALSE)
  
  dbBind(res, list("baz"))
  dbFetch(res) # <- Should be dbGetRowsAffected()
}

fetch_bound_statement(RSQLite::SQLite())
#> Warning in result_fetch(res@ptr, n = n): SQL statements must be issued with
#> dbExecute() or dbSendStatement() instead of dbGetQuery() or dbSendQuery().
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows
```

The duckdb driver gives a slightly different warning which got me on track in the end:

``` r
fetch_bound_statement(duckdb::duckdb())
#> Warning in dbFetch(res): Should not call dbFetch() on results that do not come
#> from SELECT, got INSERT
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows
```

Ideally I’d like to hear something like “use `dbGetRowsAffected()` instead”.

title: Unexpected message and test skipping when using `extended_types = TRUE`
description:
I'm using RSQLite as the backend data store/access for a package designed to retrieve and access some fish data. When running tests, which involve creating the database using RSQLite as part of the setup, I saw some strange output (` {.fn {top_level_fun}} needs the {.pkg {.val  {pkgs_not_installed}}} package{?s}.` and noticed that most of my tests were being skipped. You can recreate the behavior by doing the below - my apologies for the complexity I'm not sure if I could recreate it outside of the packaging context.

I believe that the cryptic message itself is generated [here](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/blob/eb200266eaaa6a1fa83ec5e73770c8b9c7f01914/R/import-standalone-check_suggested.R#L63), and the actual problem is that I didn't have the `hms` package installed, which [this line](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/blob/35855bbc5b19f2b907108e43684f535e689ac24c/R/dbConnect_SQLiteDriver.R#L109) checks for. Additionally, I think that `dbConnect` is not a package anymore? 

Finally, I also question whether it is appropriate to force users to skip tests - had we not had other tests failing downstream because of the earlier skipped setup tasks, we might not have realized that all of our tests were being skipped on GHA.

In the end, I was able to resolve the issue by adding `hms` to Suggests. However, this behavior seems not ideal and it took me forever to figure out what the heck was happening, so I thought I'd bring it to your attention.

### Reprex

```r
# from outside a project
remove.packages("hms")
usethis::create_package("testRSQLbug")
# switch to testRSQLbug project
usethis::use_package("RSQLite")
usethis::use_package("DBI")
usethis::use_testthat()
usethis::use_test("test_connect")
```

```r
test_that("test connect", {
    mydb <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "my-db.sqlite", extended_types = TRUE)
    expect_s4_class(mydb, "SQLiteConnection")
    DBI::dbDisconnect(mydb)
})
```

output from testing

```
==> devtools::test()

ℹ Testing testRSQbug
✔ | F W  S  OK | Context
✔ |      1   0 | test_package_loading                        

══ Results ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
── Skipped tests (1) ────────────────────────────────────────
• {.fn {top_level_fun}} needs the {.pkg {.val
  {pkgs_not_installed}}} package{?s}. (1):

[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 1 | PASS 0 ]
```

```r
library(DBI)

dbDisconnect(conn)
```

```
conn <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbFile, ...)
```

title: `PRIMARY KEY` variable is not being recognised as primary index
description:
I am not sure if this is an issue of {RSQLite} or {DBI}. However, I created an SQLite database and a table using SQL calls, even though I have declared a variable as `PRIMARY KEY`, the database does not automatically recognise it as `PRIMARY INDEX`.

## Example 1
Simple reproducible example

```r
# Setup
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)

# Create a SQLite database
con <-
  DBI::dbConnect(
    RSQLite::SQLite(),
    here::here("testA.sqlite")
  )

# Make a new table using SQL call
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  'CREATE TABLE "Datasets" (
  "dataset_id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  "dataset_name" TEXT
);'
)
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows

# Check that the table has been created
DBI::dbListTables(con)
#> [1] "Datasets"

# Check the content of the table
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  'SELECT * FROM "Datasets";'
)
#> [1] dataset_id   dataset_name
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

# Check the Primary key
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "PRAGMA index_list('Datasets');"
)
#> [1] seq     name    unique  origin  partial
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

# Manualy create the primary key
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "CREATE UNIQUE INDEX dataset_id ON Datasets(dataset_id);"
)

# Check again if the Primary key is present
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "PRAGMA index_list('Datasets');"
)
#>   seq       name unique origin partial
#> 1   0 dataset_id      1      c       0

Created on 2024-08-22 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/)
```

However, the PRIMARY KEY is automatically increased by integers but still not recognised as PRIMARY INDEX
## Example 2
```r
# Setup
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(here)

# Create a SQLite database
con <-
  DBI::dbConnect(
    RSQLite::SQLite(),
    here::here("testB.sqlite")
  )

# Make a new table using SQL call
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  'CREATE TABLE "Samples" (
  "sample_id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  "sample_name" TEXT
);'
)
#> data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows

# Check that the table has been created
DBI::dbListTables(con)
#> [1] "Samples"

# Add some data to the table
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  'INSERT INTO "Samples" ("sample_name") VALUES ("Sample1");'
)

# Check the Primary key
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "PRAGMA index_list('Datasets');"
)
#> [1] seq     name    unique  origin  partial
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

# Check the content of the table
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  'SELECT * FROM "Samples";'
)
#>   sample_id sample_name
#> 1         1     Sample1

Created on 2024-08-22 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/)
```

title: Calling internal SQLite functions to check transaction state
description:
I am looking for a way to check whether a transaction is active on my current connection.

I don't think there are any SQL statements for this, only internal functions such as [sqlite3_txn_state](https://sqlite.org/draft/c3ref/txn_state.html). (added in [v3.34](https://www.sqlite.org/releaselog/3_34_0.html))

title: RSQLite keeps numeric of epoch day as date in SQLite database whereas SQLite regards numeric as Julian day (REAL) or epoch second (INTEGER)
description:
Hi, I love shiny with RSQLite as well as light weight SQLite. Thank you for this useful package. 

Here I'd comment an apparent discrepancy of data type of date between R and SQLite. This is related but different from the issue of `extended_types = TRUE`. Also this is different from discussion about keeping date as ISO8601 string like "2012-03-04" but not numeric (https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/issues/351). 

In short, present situation is that RSQLite saves epoch ***day*** in SQLite3, which is regarded on SQLite3 as julian day by default. 
I wonder it would be more consistent if RSQLite converts R's Date object of epoch ***day*** to julian day (or less preferably epoch ***second***; \#) before inserting the data into the backend corresponding table of SQLite's database (\# note SQLite `auto` does not work as expected for data of epoch second for early 1970 because a second in range of 0-5373484.499999 is regarded as julian day, and also does not work as expected for data of julian day for older than B.C. 4714-11-24 (-4713-11-24) or newer than A.D. 9999-12-31 because such day is regarded as epoch second). 
Then, to see on SQLite what date it is in human readable format, we just need like 
```
select date(mydate) from t1 where date(mydate) = "2012-03-04";
``` 
instead of present style like 
```
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") = "2012-03-04";
```
or
```
-- For where clause, calculate based on epoch second at right-side value. 
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where mydate = unixepoch("2012-03-04") / 24/3600;
```
or
```
-- For where clause, calculate based on julian day at right-side value.
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where mydate = julianday("2012-03-04") - julianday("1970-01-01");
```

c.f. SQLite [2.2. Date and Time Datatype](https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html#date_and_time_datatype)

>2.2. Date and Time Datatype
>
>SQLite does not have a storage class set aside for storing dates and/or times. Instead, the built-in Date And Time Functions of SQLite are capable of storing dates and times as TEXT, REAL, or INTEGER values:
>
>TEXT as ISO8601 strings ("YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.SSS").
REAL as Julian day numbers, the number of days since noon in Greenwich on November 24, 4714 B.C. according to the proleptic Gregorian calendar.
INTEGER as Unix Time, the number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.
Applications can choose to store dates and times in any of these formats and freely convert between formats using the built-in date and time functions.


---

#### Brief explanation
RSQLite keeps epoch ***day*** as date in SQLite database, as R's `Date` object is epoch day. 
c.f. 
[as.Date: Date Conversion Functions to and from Character](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/as.Date)
[Connect to an SQLite database / Extended Types](https://rsqlite.r-dbi.org/reference/SQLite.html#extended-types)

SQLite handles three types as date, ISO-8601 format text, julian day, or epoch ***second***. 
The default modifier `auto` of `date()` in SQLite handles if the value is between 0.0 and 5373484.499999, then it is interpreted as a julian day number (corresponding to dates between -4713-11-24 12:00:00 and 9999-12-31 23:59:59, inclusive).
c.f. 
[2.2. Date and Time Datatype](https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html#date_and_time_datatype)
[Date And Time Functions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_datefunc.html#overview)

So, what happens when we create a date column via RSQLite in a table of SQLite3 database? RSQLite saves epoch day in SQLite3, which SQLite3 regards as julian day by default. To see on SQLite what date it is in human readable format, we need explicit multiplication by `*24*3600` along with addition of modifier "unixepoch", like
```
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") = "2012-03-04";
```
For example, in my test data below, R's Date of "2012-03-04" keeps it as epoch day, i.e. 15403, and then SQLite regards it as julian day, so SQLite gives "-4670-01-26" when "select date(mydate) from t1;".

I posted this issue on Posit Community here: 
https://forum.posit.co/t/where-can-i-find-a-document-that-tells-we-need-explicit-as-character-when-we-use-input-of-dateinput-as-parameterized-sqlite3-query-via-rsqlite-but-not-with-query-constructed-with-insecure-paste0/186415/2

#### Reprex
Here let us create SQLite database `t.db` (not on memory) via RSQLite, and then examine the data from R and from SQLite.

```
library(DBI)

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "t.db", extended_types = TRUE)
dbExecute(con, 'CREATE TABLE t1 (mydate DATE, id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);')
dbExecute(con, 'INSERT OR IGNORE INTO t1 (mydate) VALUES (?), (?);', c(as.Date("2012-03-04"), as.Date("1234-05-06")))

date1 <- as.Date("2012-03-04")
dput(date1)
# structure(15403, class = "Date")

query <- "select * from t1 where t1.mydate = ?"
dbGetQuery(con, query, params = c(date1))
#      mydate id
# 1 2012-03-04  1

dbDisconnect(con)
```
So, on R, we can see `mydate` is shown as `2012-03-04` as expected. 
(Note that I added `extended_types = TRUE` in `dbConnect()` at the beginning to get returned results as R's `Date` object which `RSQLite` correctly shows as human-readable format.) 

But on SQLite, the data inserted by RSQlite as date is indeed a small integer of epoch day, which SQLite regards as julian day by default. So we need multiplication by `*24*3600` and modifier `unixepoch` explicitly.

On terminal, 
```
sqlite3 --header t.db  
```

Then on sqlite3 console, 
\# below, `--` indicates comment line on sqlite. 

```
select * from t1;
-- mydate|id
-- 15403|1
-- -268693|2
-- The date records inserted by RSQLite are kept as small integer that is epoch day. 

select date(mydate) from t1;
-- date(mydate)
-- -4670-01-26
-- 
-- The integer is regarded as julian day at SQLite side by default, 
--  which makes "2012-03-04" to "-4670-01-26". 
-- It seems SQLite fails to judge negative small integer as epoch second for the second record (originally "1234-05-06"), 
--  although it says "If the time-value is numeric (the DDDDDDDDDD format) then the 'auto' modifier causes the time-value to interpreted as either a julian day number or a unix timestamp, depending on its magnitude." https://www.sqlite.org/lang_datefunc.html#modifiers ..

-- Adding modifier "unixepoch" along with multiplication explicitly to get desired result. 
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1;
-- date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch")
-- 2012-03-04
-- 1234-05-06
-- Here it works as described in SQLite's document as: 
--  "The "unixepoch" modifier (20) only works if it immediately follows a time-value in the DDDDDDDDDD format. This modifier causes the DDDDDDDDDD to be interpreted not as a Julian day number as it normally would be, but as Unix Time - the number of seconds since 1970. " https://www.sqlite.org/lang_datefunc.html#modifiers

-- We need it in both select and where clauses. 
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") = "2012-03-04";
-- date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch")
-- 2012-03-04

-- Or if you prefer doing at right-side value, these work. 
-- Calculation based on epoch second. 
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where mydate = unixepoch("2012-03-04") / 24/3600;
-- date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch")
-- 2012-03-04

-- Calculation based on julian day.
select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1 where mydate = julianday("2012-03-04") - julianday("1970-01-01");
-- date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch")
-- 2012-03-04

.q
```

<details>
<summary> Log with SQLite 3.43.2.  </summary>

```
% sqlite3 --header t.db      
SQLite version 3.43.2 2023-10-10 13:08:14
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
sqlite> select * from t1;
mydate|id

-268693|2

sqlite> select date(mydate) from t1;

sqlite> -- add modifier "unixepoch" along with multiplication explicitly to get desired result. 
sqlite> select date(mydate *24*3600, "unixepoch") from t1;
```

title: dbAppendTable takes ~ 30 seconds in Snowflake
description:
There seems to be some sort of constant time work happening.  The amount of time whether 5 records or 5000 records remains around 30 seconds. 

In Snowflake: 
```
create schema r_testing;

create or replace TABLE R_TESTING.TINY (
    PRODUCT_ID NUMERIC
);
```
In R:
```
con <- dbConnect()

df <- data.frame(PRODUCT_ID=1:5)

dbAppendTable(con, "TINY", df)

```

title: dbAppendTable() with SnowFlake doesn't respect DB or Schema constraints.
description:
Unfortunately there's no separate Snowflake back-end I could find. 

When using DBI and Snowflake, dbAppendTable() gets weird if the same table exists in any other schema, including a schema in a different database.  

Oddly, query functions work correctly.  This problem seems specific to dbAppendTable()

Prepare, in SQL: 
```
#
# Do this in Snowflake
#
create schema r_testing;
create schema r_testing_second;

create or replace TABLE R_TESTING.TINY (
    PRODUCT_ID NUMERIC
);

create or replace TABLE R_TESTING_SECOND.TINY (
    PRODUCT_ID NUMERIC
);
```
In R: 
```
df <- data.frame(PRODUCT_ID=1:5)

con <- DBI::dbConnect( ..... , Schema = "R_TESTING", ...)
#
# This will fail with a meaningless message (another related issue)
#
dbAppendTable( con, "TINY", df)

# Error in result_describe_parameters(rs@ptr, fieldDetails) : 
#   Query requires '1' params; '18' supplied.

#
# Workaround
#
dbAppendTable( con, SQL("R_TESTING_SECOND.TINY"), df)

# 
# If we drop either table in SQL: 
# 
#  drop TABLE R_TESTING_SECOND.TINY;

# dbAppend works 
dbAppendTable( con, "TINY", df)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

title: FR : bindings to sqlite3_clear_bindings
description:
Hi,
If I understand the SQLite doc correctly, there is a function that allows to [clear bindings](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/clear_bindings.html) after a reset and hence get a fresh renewed prepared query.
Right now, as far as I know, within RSQLité there is no way to keep a prepared query in memory. Could it be possible to make a function that calls **reset** and **clear_bindings** on the results without breaking the pointer ?

That would allow a simple way of dealing with prepared queries compiled at connection time, or as lazy singletons.
That is, if your application relies on sophisticated queries that are always the same, you just upload/prepare them once.

Thanks,
Arnaud

title: slice_sample() does not interact correctly with set.seed() when working with an SQLite database
description:
I'm not too sure if this issue sits within dbplyr or RSQLite, but the slice_sample() function does not appear to be taking account of a seed set via set.seed() when using an SQLite database.

If I set a seed, then run slice_sample(), then later set the same seed, and run slice_sample() again, the sampled table is different.

For comparison, when undertaking these sample operations using a Microsoft SQL Server database, the expected behaviour is observed (i.e., the two sampled tables are identical).

```r
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)


tbl <- tibble(n = 1:30)
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(conn, "test_table", tbl)

set.seed(100)
sample2 <- slice_sample(tbl(conn, "test_table"), n = 3)

identical(sample1, sample2)
```

title: Support encrypted databases
description:
Hi, I'm looking for a way to read encrypted sqlite databases.
There are many different ciphers allowing encryption of sqlite databases. One project support multiple ciphers: https://github.com/utelle/SQLite3MultipleCiphers

I am not a C programmer but as far I understand, SQLite3MultipleCiphers is a fork of sqlite and could be integrated in RSQLite instead of the original sqlite source code.

I guess this would allow users to decrypt database through simple dsn specification.
For example, accessing a sqlite dabase encrypted with sqlcipher is as simple as appeding the following to the dsn: `?_cipher=sqlcipher&_key=<passphrase>`.

Edit: DNS is a exposed by some libraries in other langages, but after investigation they all translate internally DNS variables to PRAGMA statements or sqlite functions. MultipleCiphers doesn't handle translation by itself.

I would perfectly understand that dropping sqlite for one of its forks may not be relevant here but maybe providing documentation on how to get it done may be usefull to some devs?

I would gladly investigate the topic if you find it relevant. Could you just just provide me clues on how to compile this package against an sqlite fork like SQLite3MultipleCiphers?

title: CAST(NULL AS type) does not cast missing data NA to the expected type
description:
It seems impossible to cast NA when a new variable containing only NA is created within SQL.  More precisely,  `CAST(expr AS type)`  in a `SELECT` query always returns logical NA  when the expression contains only NA/NULL values. 

As a result, it does not appear possible to prevent the NA type for a new variable to be `logical` if the subset of data involved in the computation has only missing data.

## Example 1

```r
library(RSQLite)
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")

# create a data frame with numeric and character NA
df <- data.frame(num=as.numeric(NA),text=as.character(NA))

# load in the data base
dbWriteTable(con, "test", value = df, overwrite = TRUE )

# NA type corresponds to column types when recovering 
rs <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM test") )
```
> str(rs)
'data.frame':   1 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ num : num NA
 $ text: chr NA

So far, it behaves as expected. See following [comment](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/issues/74#issuecomment-196423751)
>   - The first non-NULL value decides the type of the column.
>   - If all values are NULL, the result is a vector of NAs of the declared data type for the column, or logical.
```r
# compute a new variable from NA value
rs <- str( dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT num, num+1 AS new FROM test") )
```
>str(rs)
'data.frame':   1 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ num : num NA
 $ new: logi NA

When creating a new variable, the data type of the new variable is `logical`, which might be ok in this case (but this makes less sense in the second example)
```r
rs <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT CAST(num+1 AS INTEGER) AS new FROM test") 
```
> str(rs)
'data.frame':   1 obs. of  1 variable:
 $ new: logi NA

`CAST(NULL as type)` does not work in this context. The `NA` is still logical:
```r
 # Casting a new column of NA/NULL does not work
rs<- dbGetQuery(con,  "SELECT CAST(NULL AS INTEGER) AS new_num, CAST(NULL AS TEXT) new_text FROM test") 
```
> str(rs)
'data.frame':   1 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ new_num : logi NA
 $ new_text: logi NA

## Example 2

The above example is contrived but the issue of the return type for NA is particularly annoying when there is a NA is some records but not other:

```r
df2 <- data.frame(id = c(1,2),  num = c(1, NA), text = c("a", NA) )
 dbWriteTable(con, "test2", value = df2, overwrite = TRUE )

# compute some extra variables
rs <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT *, num+1 AS new_num,  text||'b' AS new_text FROM test2")
```
> str(rs)
'data.frame':   2 obs. of  5 variables:
   $ id      : num  1 2
   $ num     : num  1 NA
   $ text    : chr  "a" NA
   $ new_num : num  2 NA
   $ new_text: chr  "ab" NA

Note that the extra variables have the expected types.  However, the type is logical when the same operation is executed only on the second record:

```r
# compute some extra variables when there missing data
rs <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT *, num+1 AS new_num,  text||'b' AS new_text FROM test2 WHERE id=2")
```
> str(rs)
'data.frame':   1 obs. of  5 variables:
   $ id      : num 2
   $ num     : num NA
   $ text    : chr NA
   $ new_num : logi NA
   $ new_text: logi NA

Note that this is different from R behaviour:

```{r}
tmp <- df2[df2$id==2,]
tmp$new_num <- tmp$num+1
```
> str(tmp)
'data.frame':   1 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ id     : num 2
 $ num    : num NA
 $ text   : chr NA
 $ new_num: num NA

I understand that there is a default toward logical when a *new variable* contains only NA but I think that it should be possible  to obtain a column of the desired type even if it contains only missing data in one way or another.

title: Adding Date operations
description:
Having the extended types is great, but it seems they can only be used to put data in and get it out? Are there functions and operators in SQL that allow working with dates? (I searched, but was unable to find any documentation on this topic). For example, there does not appear to be a `DATEDIFF()` or `DATEADD()` equivalent, and casting to `DATE` has no effect:

```r
library(RSQLite)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), extended_types = TRUE)

# Cast to DATE has no effect. Note that same effect is achieved when casting to random type like 'FOOBAR'.
tibble::tibble(dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT CAST('2000-01-01' AS DATE) AS a_date;"))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#> a_date
#> <int>
#>   1   2000
# (Expected output: a variable of type Date with value '2000-01-01')


# Trying to find number of days between two dates:
dbSendStatement(con, "CREATE TABLE test (x DATE, y DATE);")
dbSendStatement(con, "INSERT INTO test (x, y) VALUES ('2000-01-01', '2000-01-03');")
tibble::tibble(dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT y - x AS delta FROM test;"))
# # A tibble: 1 x 1
# delta
# <int>
#   1     0
# (Expected output: a variable of type integer with value 2)
```

title: Remove dbFetch() warning for statements

The code below gives a dbFetch warning.  Previously that did not occur.  

sqldf does not know whether it is sending a select, create or whatever.  Would like to be able to avoid this warning.

```
library(sqldf)

set.seed(1)
n <- 100
DF1 <- data.frame(a = sample(n, n, replace = TRUE), 
   b = sample(4, n, replace = TRUE), c1 = runif(n))
DF2 <- data.frame(a = sample(n, n, replace = TRUE), 
   b = sample(4, n, replace = TRUE), c2 = runif(n))

result <- sqldf(c("create index ai2 on DF2(a, b)", 
  "select * from DF1 natural join main.DF2"), verbose = TRUE)
```
giving:
```
sqldf: library(RSQLite)
sqldf: m <- dbDriver("SQLite")
sqldf: connection <- dbConnect(m, dbname = ":memory:")
sqldf: initExtension(connection)
sqldf: dbWriteTable(connection, 'DF2', DF2, row.names = FALSE)
sqldf: dbWriteTable(connection, 'DF1', DF1, row.names = FALSE)
sqldf: dbGetQuery(connection, 'create index ai2 on DF2(a, b)')
sqldf: dbGetQuery(connection, 'select * from DF1 natural join main.DF2')
sqldf: dbDisconnect(connection)
Warning message:
In rsqlite_fetch(res@ptr, n = n) :
  Don't need to call dbFetch() for statements, only for queries
```

title: Improve error message when writing dataframe with unsupported data type
description:
I found the hard way that SQLite does not support date types. This discovery could have been short circuited had RSQLite given me useful information when I attempted to use **dbWriteTable** with a dataframe that had a POSIXlt type. The error message I get is:
```
Error in rsqlite_bind_rows(rs@ptr, value) : 
  Parameter 2 does not have length 11.
```

To make sense of this, you'd have to be intimately familiar with RSQLite's innards. That error is almost absent on Google, even when omitting the digits. Finding **rsqlite_bind_rows** in the appropriate .cpp file in this repository shed no useful light on the issue. Had I not stumbled across the answer in an unrelated exploration, problem diagnosis would have taken a long time.

Throw us a bone: if the data type in my dataframe is why the data can't be saved, please let me know this.

title: `dbGetQuery()` returns no columns for INSERT ... RETURNING on temporary tables
description:
Temporary tables return a tibble with the correct number of rows but with no columns

``` r
x <- tibble::tibble(
  x = 1:3,
  y = runif(3)
)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:", create = TRUE)
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "tbl", x)
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "INSERT INTO tbl (`x`, `y`)
   VALUES (100, 1)
   RETURNING *",
  immediate = TRUE
)
#>     x y
#> 1 100 1

DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "tmp_tbl", x, temporary = TRUE)
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "INSERT INTO tmp_tbl (`x`, `y`)
   VALUES (100, 1)
   RETURNING *",
  immediate = TRUE
)
#> data frame with 0 columns and 4 rows
```

title: `RETURNING`  produces wrong column name
description:
While working on the support for `RETURNING` in `dm::rows_insert()` https://github.com/cynkra/dm/issues/593 I noticed that the column names produced by returning are escaped

``` r
library(RSQLite)

x <- tibble::tibble(
  x = 1:3,
  y = runif(3)
)

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:", create = TRUE)
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "tbl", x, overwrite = TRUE)
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "tbl2", x, overwrite = TRUE)

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "INSERT INTO tbl (`x`, `y`)
   SELECT * FROM tbl2
   RETURNING `x`",
  immediate = TRUE
)
#>   `x`
#> 1   1
#> 2   2
#> 3   3

DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT `x` FROM tbl2",
  immediate = TRUE
)
#>   x
#> 1 1
#> 2 2
#> 3 3
```

title: Rstudio Connection pane opens also when RSQlite called from inside a function
description:
I have a package that calls different SQLite databases for caching. Starting with RSQLite 2.2.6, if I use this package in Rstudio I just see the connections pane continuosly opening and closing, with no apparent way to disable this behaviour (even if I hide this from the settings, it appears again as soon as a new connection to SQLite is made from inside a function). This is annoying, and, I suspect is the cause for otherwise unexpected `R code execution errors` that I get from the Rstudio IDE.

I am reporting this here, however, as I understand that a better implementation of the Rstudio connection contract would make it possible to have the connection pane opened only when `RSQlite` is called from outside a function. If it is called from within a function, then the pane would not appear. 

For details, see in particular [this post in the Rstudio community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/database-connections-pane/43230/2?u=giocomai), which refers to how the ODBC package [implements this](https://github.com/r-dbi/odbc/blob/7b35549f9df935e1d132f6221860f87a6eb64ef6/R/Driver.R#L115).

Shouldn't this be the default behaviour of RSQlite as well?

In brief, in a scenario such as the following, I believe the connection pane should not appear:

```r
test <- function(){
  con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
  return(con)
}
test()
```
If more examples are needed, I'm happy to provide further reference to real world scenarios, but I'm sure you can esily imagine a function working with different sqlite databases that when called leads to a whirlwind of action in the connection pane that I'm sure is undesirable for most users. 

I understand that this behaviour can be disabled with `options(connectionObserver = NULL)`, but it took more than I care to admit to find this out as it is not clearly referenced in the documentation. 

If you feel that instead the current behaviour is desirable, I would appreciate suggestions on a way for packages that depend on RSQLite to opt out of the integration with the Rstudio connections pane. Thanks!

title: CSV extension ignores schema's data type.
description:
Thanks for adding the recent extensions that support CSV imports (eg, #407, #389). 

I believe the data types passed to the `schema` argument aren't being respected.  This is from the [recent documentation](https://rsqlite.r-dbi.org/reference/initextension) (and I've added `str(ds)` to display the data types

``` r
library(DBI)
db <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite())
RSQLite::initExtension(db, "csv")
# use the filename argument to mount CSV files from disk
sql <- paste0(
  "CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE tbl USING ",
  "csv(data='1,2', schema='CREATE TABLE x(a INT, b INT)')"
)
dbExecute(db, sql)
#> [1] 0
ds <- dbGetQuery(db, "SELECT * FROM tbl")


str(ds)
#> 'data.frame':    1 obs. of  2 variables:
#>  $ a: chr "1"
#>  $ b: chr "2"
```

Version:
```r
RSQLite::rsqliteVersion()
#>   header  library 
#> "3.38.0" "3.38.0"
```

title: Feature request: Datetime Conversions
description:
This relates to #104

If I connect to a sqlite file with the windows odbc-driver [sqliteodbc](https://github.com/softace/sqliteodbc) using the DBI-driver odbc::odbc(), any column declared as 'date' in the schema gets converted to a Date column in R (cf. the README in the linked repo for mapping details), ex:

```R

library(DBI)

odbcon = dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), .connection_string="DRIVER=SQLite3 ODBC Driver;Database=:memory:")

dbExecute(odbcon, "create table t1 (dt DATE)")
dbExecute(odbcon, "insert into t1 values ('2020-01-01')")

df1 = dbGetQuery(odbcon, "select * from t1")
str(df1)
# 'data.frame':	1 obs. of  1 variable:
#  $ dt: Date, format: "2020-01-01"
```

Using RSQLite however the column is returned as-is:

```R
dbcon = dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

dbExecute(dbcon, "create table t1 (dt DATE)")
dbExecute(dbcon, "insert into t1 values ('2020-01-01')")

df2 = dbGetQuery(dbcon, "select * from t1")
str(df2)
# 'data.frame':	1 obs. of  1 variable:
#  $ dt: chr "2020-01-01"
```


It would be nice if a column declared as 'date' in the table schema could be automatically converted to the 'Date' class in R. Similarly for datetime /POSIXct and time/hms(or difftime), and even boolean/logical.

title: Parameterised queries cannot return correct order by using `ORDER BY`
description:
I find the parameterised queries by `dbBind` or `dbGetQuery(...,  params = mylist)` cannot return a correct ordered result.  

Example:
```r
library("RSQLite")

conn1 <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "ex1.db")
dbExecute(conn1, "CREATE TABLE mydata (_pkey INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);")
dfr <- data.frame(name = c("a", "a", "b", "c", "b", "c", "e"))
dbAppendTable(conn1, "mydata", dfr)
```
Correct query:

```r
dbGetQuery(conn1, paste0("SELECT _pkey, name FROM mydata WHERE _pkey < 8 AND name IN ('e', 'a', 'b') ",
                         "ORDER BY CASE name WHEN 'e' THEN 1 ",
                         "WHEN 'a' THEN 2 ",
                         "WHEN 'b' THEN 3 END"))
  _pkey name
1     7    e
2     1    a
3     2    a
4     3    b
5     5    b
```

But when using prepared statements, the table isn't in the correct order:

```r
rs <- dbSendQuery(conn1, paste0("SELECT _pkey, name FROM mydata WHERE _pkey = $pkey AND name IN ('e', 'a', 'b') ",
                                "ORDER BY CASE name WHEN 'e' THEN 1 ",
                                "WHEN 'a' THEN 2 ",
                                "WHEN 'b' THEN 3 END"))
dbBind(rs, list(pkey = seq(7L)))
res <- dbFetch(rs)
res
  _pkey name
1     1    a
2     2    a
3     3    b
4     5    b
5     7    e
```

I prefer to use prepared statement in my code, since I have to deal with a huge table with RAM usage issues.

title: dbAppendTable is slow while dbWriteTable is fast
description:
`dbAppendTable()` is very slow on a file. It is fast for the in-memory DB. 

``` r

tab <- pkgcache::meta_cache_list()

## Remove the list columns
tab <- tab[, !sapply(tab, is.list)]
dim(tab)
#> [1] 35359    31

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), tempfile(), create = TRUE)
system.time(DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "pkgs", tab))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.162   0.043   0.211
dim(DBI::dbReadTable(con, "pkgs"))
#> [1] 35359    31
rm(con)

con2 <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), tempfile(), create = TRUE)
DBI::dbCreateTable(con2, "pkgs", tab)
dim(DBI::dbReadTable(con2, "pkgs"))
#> [1]  0 31
system.time(DBI::dbAppendTable(con2, "pkgs", tab))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   1.122  11.886  15.088
dim(DBI::dbReadTable(con2, "pkgs"))
#> [1] 35359    31
```

title: help needed for blob
description:

I have tried some google commands with serialize but failed to get a working command set.

```
conn <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), paste0(DBpath, "/", DBfile))
file <- "/path/to/some/file.pdf"
fcontent <- readBin(con = file, what = raw(), n = file.info(file)$size)
content <- serialize(fcontent, NULL)  
pid=1 # for testing

                            "'", ext, "', ",
                            "'", content, "' ",
                            ")")
res <- dbSendQuery(conn, query)
dbClearResult(res)
```

Thanks

title: Database keeps locking on Ubuntu
description:
Hi all, 

I am using Ubuntu 16.04 (can't upgrade as this is a virtual machine at my university), RSQLite (2.2.0), R version 3.6.2. 

---

The following code works fine on my personal mac but throws 

```
Error: database is locked
Error: database is locked
```
on the Ubuntu machine. 

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(dbplyr)


db_file <- "foo.db"
db <- RSQLite::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), db_file)

foo <- data.frame(a=1:50000, b=1:50000)
```

title: Coerce POSIXct to julian date when writing
description:
``` r
library(DBI)

df <- data.frame(date = ISOdate(2016, 1, 1:5))
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(con, "df", df)

# Date time functions don't work
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT date, date(date) FROM df")
#>         date date(date)
#> 1 1451649600         NA
#> 2 1451736000         NA
#> 3 1451822400         NA
#> 4 1451908800         NA
#> 5 1451995200         NA

# But they do if we convert to Julian data time
offset <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT julianday('1970-01-01 12:00')")[[1]]

df2 <- data.frame(date = as.numeric(julian(df$date) + offset - 1))
dbWriteTable(con, "df2", df2, overwrite = TRUE)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT date, date(date), time(date) FROM df2")
#>      date date(date) time(date)
#> 1 2457388 2016-01-01   00:00:00
#> 2 2457390 2016-01-02   00:00:00
#> 3 2457390 2016-01-03   00:00:00
#> 4 2457392 2016-01-04   00:00:00
```

title: Date type support in DBWriteTable
description:
Thank you very much for adding Date support in RSQLite! RSQLite support Date typed columns when tables are created using SQL. However when tables are created from dataframes using dbWriteTable Date types are converted to numbers. My expectation is that when creating a SQLite table from a dataframe with `dbWriteTable` that Date types would be preserved and not converted to numbers.

``` r
library(RSQLite)
#> Warning: package 'RSQLite' was built under R version 4.0.4

conn <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), extended_types = TRUE)

myTable <- data.frame(someDate = as.Date(c("2000-01-01", "2000-02-03")),
                      someNumber = c(1,2))                           


# dbWriteTable will convert Dates to numeric type
dbWriteTable(conn, "my_table", myTable)
dbReadTable(conn, "my_table")
#>   someDate someNumber
#> 1    10957          1
#> 2    10990          2
class(dbReadTable(conn, "my_table")$someDate)
#> [1] "numeric"


# Date types are created when using SQL to create a table
dbExecute(conn, "CREATE TABLE my_table_2 (some_date DATE);")
#> [1] 0
dbExecute(conn, "INSERT INTO my_table_2 values ('2000-01-01'), ('2000-02-03');")
#> [1] 2

dbGetQuery(conn, 'SELECT * from my_table_2')
#>    some_date
#> 1 2000-01-01
#> 2 2000-02-03
class(dbGetQuery(conn, 'SELECT * from my_table_2')$some_date)
#> [1] "Date"


# Dates do not get converted when using dplyr::copy_to
dplyr::copy_to(conn, myTable, "my_table_3")
dplyr::tbl(conn, "my_table_3")
#> # Source:   table<my_table_3> [?? x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.34.1 []
#>   someDate someNumber
#>      <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1    10957          1
#> 2    10990          2

dbDisconnect(conn)
```

title: Valid field.types parameter passed to dbWriteTable raises error
description:
Between v2.1.0 and v2.1.1 it appears that validation was added to the dbWriteTable function (in table.R) to ensure field.types is a character vector. However, it looks like there may be a problem with this validation when a list (rather than the default 'NULL') is supplied as the parameter.

In v2.0 this worked: 
```R
DBI::dbWriteTable(conn,name="mytable",value=my.dataframe, field.types=list(term_id="COLLATE BINARY",term_status="",term_30="",term_60="",term_198=""),overwrite=TRUE,header=FALSE,row.names=FALSE)
``` 

But in v2.2 I now receive the error: 
```
`field.types` must be a named character vector with unique names, or NULL
```

Looking at the code it seems that this block in table.R:
```R
if (!is.null(field.types) && !(is.character(field.types) && !is.null(names(field.types)) && !anyDuplicated(names(field.types)))) {
      stopc("`field.types` must be a named character vector with unique names, or NULL")
    }
```

Could be changed to this. This would handle duplicates and non-lists:
```R
if (!is.null(field.types) && !is.list(field.types) || anyDuplicated(names(field.types))) {
      stopc("`field.types` must be a named character vector with unique names, or NULL")
    }
```
I would be happy to create a pull request for this if you agree with the change.

title: Mangling of duplicated colnames in data frames resulting from a query breaks Bioconductor packages
description:
Hi,

We just released BioC 3.7 a few days ago (on May 1st) and several packages broke already because of this change in RSQLite 2.1.1:

  _Data frames resulting from a query always have unique non-empty column names (r-dbi/DBItest#137)._

I see that the issue was discussed here https://github.com/r-dbi/DBItest/issues/137

It's a little bit disappointing that this kind of breaking changes are made without more consideration for the existing packages. If only it was an improvement but name mangling has always proven to be an annoyance more than anything else. Furthermore, the fact that RSQLite uses its own mangling (via internal helper `tidy_names`) instead of `base::make.names()` adds another layer of inconsistency and confusion.

Could this at least be made optional e.g. via a new argument to `dbGetQuery` and `dbFetch` (and possibly to a few other functions)? Or is there an easy and robust way to bring the original names back if one wishes to (removing the `..n` suffix is not robust). Thanks!

H.

title: Column name mangling in RSQLite >= 2.1.1
description:
After _column name mangling_ was introduced in RSQLite 2.1.1 (May 2018), with no consultation with the Bioconductor community (who's been maintaining and using the package for many years before this change, and who still heavily relies on it), and with no option to turn it off, I opened issue #259 to report that the change broke many Bioconductor packages and to argue against such change.

2 days ago issue #259 was closed [claiming](https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/issues/259#issuecomment-570815276) that the _column name mangling_ feature had been removed. But AFAICS it has not:
```
library(RSQLite)
conn <- dbConnect(SQLite())
df <- data.frame(aa=1:5, bb=11:15)
dbWriteTable(conn, "toto", df)
dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT *, aa FROM toto")
#   aa bb aa..3
# 1  1 11     1
# 2  2 12     2
# 3  3 13     3
# 4  4 14     4
# 5  5 15     5
```
This is with DBI_1.1.0.9000 and RSQLite_2.1.5.9000 (latest versions available thru `install_github()`). See my `sessionInfo()` below.

My view on _column name mangling_  has not changed: I still consider it a bad feature. This is because it does not respect the user intention. In my `"SELECT *, aa FROM toto"` query I'm requesting that the last column of the result should be the `aa` column **and** that this column should be named `aa`.  If I wanted it to be named otherwise, I would have said so by using `AS` in my query. Note that, because of the stubborn _column name mangling_, even using `AS` won't always give me what I'm asking for:
```
dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT *,aa AS bb FROM toto")
#   aa bb bb..3
# 1  1 11     1
# 2  2 12     2
# 3  3 13     3
# 4  4 14     4
# 5  5 15     5
```
Respecting the user choice is a fundamental principle of good software design. This is why features like `stringAsFactors` and _column name mangling_ are bad.

After many years, the R core people have finally started to change their mind about the pertinence of the `stringAsFactors` feature and they're now in the process of reverting it back. This is good news. Hopefully the same thing will happen with _column name mangling_ in RSQLite.

One more thing: as already reported in issue #259 the current mangling scheme is broken if some column names have a `..n` suffix (which you can NOT assume will never happen):
```
dbWriteTable(conn, "foo", data.frame(`aa..5`=11:13, `bb`=21:23, check.names=FALSE))
dbWriteTable(conn, "bar", data.frame(`bb`=22:24, `aa..6`=42:44, check.names=FALSE))
dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT * FROM foo JOIN bar ON (foo.bb=bar.bb)")
#   aa..1 bb bb..3 aa..4
# 1    12 22    22    42
# 2    13 23    23    43
```
One should be able to identify column names that have been mangled and recover the original names. This is not the case here. So if for some reason you still believe _column name mangling_ is a good feature, at least please fix it. 

Thanks!

title: REGEXP with RSQLite
description:
I am trying to load the regexp.dll library which I compiled with GCC into RSQLite. The regexp.c extension is available in SQLite source.

The extensions is compiled like this:

`gcc ./ext/misc/regexp.c -shared -o ./../export/regexp.dll`

I can load this into my own compiled SQLite CLI, but I cannot load it into RSQLite. Without cygwin1.dll, I get the error: "The specified module could not be found". With cygwin1.dll in PATH the R session crashes. What is going on here?

Can this library not simply be statically linked with RSQLite? Separately compiling and loading these functions is a pain, especially on different platforms.

Cf: https://github.com/rstats-db/RSQLite/issues/85

title: duplicated column names
description:
This gives an error which is not easily understandable as being caused by duplicate column names. Not sure if it is worth it to address it or if it would be better done in the SQLite code.  

```
library(RSQLite)
dd <- data.frame(1,2)
names(dd) <- c("a", "a")

con <- dbConnect(SQLite())
dbWriteTable(con, "dd", dd)
```

If one uses RH2 and the H2 database similar code does give an understandable error message identifying the problem as a duplicated column name and identifying the dupliated column name.

```
library(RH2)
con <- dbConnect(H2())
dbWriteTable(con, "dd", dd) # dd defined above
```

title: (dbplyr): mutate(round) quietly clobbers non-numeric columns
description:
Re-filed by request from [`dplyr` 2908](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2908).

I have only tested this using RSQLite (so I don't know if it applies to other databases or not), but `dplyr`/`dbplyr` quietly applies round() to non-numeric columns.  The expected behavior (which is also safe and desirable) would be more like what happens with local `data.frame`s: the rounding errors out when it hits non-numeric columns.

reprex:

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library("dplyr"))
packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.7.1.9000'
packageVersion("dbplyr")
#> [1] '1.0.0.9000'
packageVersion("RSQlite")
#> [1] '2.0'
packageVersion("magrittr")
#> [1] '1.5'
base::date()
#> [1] "Sat Jun 24 09:58:25 2017"

db <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), 
                     ":memory:")
dL <- data.frame(x = 3.077, 
                 k = 'a', 
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dR <- dplyr::copy_to(db, dL, 'dR')

dR %>% mutate_all(funs(round(., 2)))
#> # Source:   lazy query [?? x 2]
#> # Database: sqlite 3.19.3 [:memory:]
#>       x     k
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  3.08     0
```

Example of desired behavior (an exception warning the user):

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library("dplyr"))

dL <- data.frame(x = 3.077, 
                 k = 'a', 
                 stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dL %>% mutate_all(funs(round(., 2)))
#> Error in mutate_impl(.data, dots): Evaluation error: non-numeric argument to mathematical function.
```

title: Domain error occurs in R but not in SQLite Manager
description:
I run a SQL statement via RSQLite over a local sqlite3 database:

``` SQL
SELECT * FROM
    (SELECT Stkcd1, Stkcd2,
        ((psum-(sum1*sum2/n))*(psum-(sum1*sum2/n)))/((sum1sq-sum1*sum1/n)*(sum2sq-sum2*sum2/n))) AS corr,
        n FROM
        (SELECT c1.Stkcd AS Stkcd1, c2.Stkcd AS Stkcd2,
            SUM(t1.Adjprcwd) AS sum1,
            SUM(t2.Adjprcwd) AS sum2,
            SUM(t1.Adjprcwd*t1.Adjprcwd) AS sum1sq,
            SUM(t2.Adjprcwd*t2.Adjprcwd) AS sum2sq,
            SUM(t1.Adjprcwd*t2.Adjprcwd) AS psum,
            COUNT(*) AS n FROM SCompany AS c1, SCompany AS c2,
            CTick AS t1, CTick AS t2
        WHERE c1.Stkcd < c2.Stkcd AND
            c1.Stkcd = t1.Stkcd AND
            c2.Stkcd = t2.Stkcd AND
            t1.Trddt = t2.Trddt
        GROUP BY c1.Stkcd, c2.Stkcd)
        )
    WHERE ABS(corr)>=%f AND n>=%d
    ORDER BY ABS(corr) DESC
    LIMIT %d
```

In the statement, I calculate the correlation of two time series and aggregate the data by correlations. %f, %d will be replaced by `sprintf` function in R. Although the SQL currently looks stupid and of low efficiency, it should work both in R and SQLite Manager with the same results.

However, an error occurs when RSQLite runs:
Error in sqliteFetch(rs, n = -1, ...) : 
  RSQLite driver: (RS_SQLite_fetch: failed first step: Domain error)

I don't know how I should debug the code in R, so I run the same code with parameters replaced in SQLite Manager in Firefox. It perfectly worked. But the same code simply does not work in RSQLite. I don't know what "Domain error" means and there seems to be little information online about this error.

Anyone has an idea what might be the problem? Or how should I debug the error?

title: OO proposal
description:
To make for a simple design, I suggest we further reduce the use of multiple inheritance, instead replacing it with composition. Currently, SQLiteObject is used as a base class underlying all three main classes (driver, connection and results).  This is not great because it forces the use of multiple inheritance (which makes method dispatch harder to predict) and it's only providing a very thin wrapper around an external pointer (and the type of the object that that points to is different in each case).

This change would mean the every old method definition for SQLiteObject would need to be duplicated three times, but that's just show, dbDataType, make.db.names, isSQLKeyword and SQLKeywords.

title: Temporary tables and inferred type for RSQLite
description:
This issue was received by email to the maintainer:

Try this self contained code with the github version of RSQLite.
Column b seems to be copied correctly from dd to ddt but column a
(which has an NA) is converted to character but should not be.
Regards.

```
> library(RSQLite)
> con <- dbConnect(SQLite())
> dd <- data.frame(a = c(NA, 3.5), b = c(1.5, 2.5))
> dbWriteTable(con, "dd", dd, row.names = FALSE)
[1] TRUE
> dbGetQuery(con, "create temporary table ddt(a, b)")
NULL
> dbGetQuery(con, "insert into ddt select * from dd")
NULL
> str(dbGetQuery(con, "select * from dd"))
'data.frame':   2 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ a: num  NA 3.5
 $ b: num  1.5 2.5
> str(dbGetQuery(con, "select * from ddt"))
'data.frame':   2 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ a: chr  NA "3.5"
 $ b: num  1.5 2.5
```

RSQLite guesses the type of columns using a heuristic. The schema of the table is consulted, if available. Otherwise, the first row of the result set is used. This is imperfect, but allows for more efficient code.

I suspect what's happening here is that the way the temp table is created, doesn't capture the same schema details.

title: Bigint handling
description:
(I sent the message below to Seth Falcon, adding it here so it does not get lost)

I recently had a problem with importing a sqlite DB table through your package. The sqlite DB contained apparently 8 byte "bigints" which RSQLite than happily converted to R integers and overflowing values. I only noticed that because all values should have been > 0, but I encountered negative values in R.

I solved this problem be explicitly casting these fields to double in my SELECT statement.

Note that I understand that such large INTS cannot (currently) be represented in R and I am not complaining about having to do that cast, but I find it worrisome and error-prone that the above mentioned internal conversion is performed without any error or warning. I also could not find a hint in the documentation about this, maybe this would help other users?

title: dbWriteTable cannot be nested within a transaction
description:
`dbWriteTable` uses `dbBegin` ... `dbCommit` but these do not nest so `dbWriteTable` cannot be within a larger transaction.

These should be changed to use SQLite savepoints as those can be nested.

```
dbGetQuery(con, "savepoint dbWriteTable")
....
dbGetQuery(con, "release dbWriteTable")
```

For more info see: http://sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html

Hi, 

When applying the dbSendQuery() function to modify values from a primary key of a parent table, the related value in the child table is not updated in cascade. Any explanations ? 

Thanks in advance

Clement

library(RSQLite)

dbListTables(db)
## Create tables

  artistid    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, 
  artistname  TEXT
);")

  trackid     INTEGER,
  trackname   TEXT, 
  trackartist INTEGER REFERENCES artist(artistid) ON UPDATE CASCADE
);")
## Fill values in the tables

dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO artist VALUES(1, 'tutu')")
dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO artist VALUES(2, 'toto')")
dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO artist VALUES(3, 'lulu')")
dbGetQuery(db, "select \* from artist")

dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO track VALUES(1, 'track1', 1)")
dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO track VALUES(2, 'track2', 1)")
dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO track VALUES(3, 'track3', 1)")
dbSendQuery(db, "INSERT INTO track VALUES(4, 'track1', 2)")

dbGetQuery(db, "select \* from track")

dbDisconnect(db)

title: text column values read as raw
description:
Hi,

WIth the following sqlite3 database:

https://s3.amazonaws.com/rsqlite-text-problem/annotationhub.sqlite3

And the following code:

```
library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "annotationhub.sqlite3")
```

   dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT description FROM resources LIMIT 3");

The result is

```
         description
1 46, 41, 53, 54, 41, 20, 44, 4e, 41, 20, 73, 65, 71, 75, 65, 6e, 63, 65, 20, 66, 6f, 72, 20, 41, 69, 6c, 75, 72, 6f, 70, 6f, 64, 61, 20, 6d, 65, 6c, 61, 6e, 6f, 6c, 65, 75, 63, 61
2 46, 41, 53, 54, 41, 20, 44, 4e, 41, 20, 73, 65, 71, 75, 65, 6e, 63, 65, 20, 66, 6f, 72, 20, 41, 69, 6c, 75, 72, 6f, 70, 6f, 64, 61, 20, 6d, 65, 6c, 61, 6e, 6f, 6c, 65, 75, 63, 61
3 46, 41, 53, 54, 41, 20, 44, 4e, 41, 20, 73, 65, 71, 75, 65, 6e, 63, 65, 20, 66, 6f, 72, 20, 41, 69, 6c, 75, 72, 6f, 70, 6f, 64, 61, 20, 6d, 65, 6c, 61, 6e, 6f, 6c, 65, 75, 63, 61
```

And yet 'description' is defined as a text file; in the sqlite3 shell:

```
sqlite> .sch resources
CREATE TABLE `resources` (`id` integer NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, `ah_id` varchar(255) NOT NULL, `title` varchar(255), `dataprovider` varchar(255), `species` varchar(255), `taxonomyid` integer, `genome` varchar(255), `description` text, `coordinate_1_based` boolean, `maintainer` varchar(255), `status_id` integer, `location_prefix_id` integer, `recipe_id` integer, `rdatadateadded` date, `rdatadateremoved` date, `record_id` integer, `preparerclass` varchar(255));
```

And the equivalent query in the shell returns text as expected:

```
sqlite> select description from resources limit 3;
FASTA DNA sequence for Ailuropoda melanoleuca
FASTA DNA sequence for Ailuropoda melanoleuca
FASTA DNA sequence for Ailuropoda melanoleuca
```

If it helps, I think I know what caused the database to get into the state where RSQLite is seeing the description field as raw, but I'm not sure why it's happening or whose fault it is.
The database was a MySQL database, and I first ran a (ruby) [Sequel](http://sequel.jeremyevans.net/) migration on it to change the type of the description column from varchar(255) to text; this should be equivalent to running an `alter table` query. Then I converted the MySQL database to sqlite, also using Sequel:

```
sequel mysql://user:password@host/annotationhub -C sqlite://annotationhub.sqlite3
```

After doing this, I get the results above. 
I should note that I did not have this problem when the description column was a varchar(255).

If I reverse the migration (changing description's type from text back to varchar(255)) and re-convert the MySQL database to sqlite again, the code above works fine. 

One theory was that somehow there was non-ascii content in the database so it was read in as a raw vector instead of a character vector. But the content of the database has not changed, just the data type of one column. 

Using Sequel for migrations and converting the MySQL database to sqlite is part of an established workflow and I would prefer not to change it if at all possible.

Any ideas? Thanks.

title: Probably should upgrade to SQlite 3.8.10.2
description:
From the news: https://www.sqlite.org/news.html

> Yikes! Index corruption after a sequence of valid SQL statements!
> 
> It has been many years since anything like this bug has snuck into an official SQLite release. But for the pasts seven months (version 3.8.7 through version **3.8.10.1**) if you do an INSERT into a carefully crafted schema in which there are two nested triggers that convert an index key value from TEXT to INTEGER and then back to TEXT again, the INTEGER value might get inserted as the index key instead of the correct TEXT, resulting in index corruption. This patch release adds a single line of code to fix the problem.
> 
> If you do actually encounter this problem, running REINDEX on the damaged indexes will clear it.

title: Errors in params list are 0-indexed
description:
When a params list to a db query has an error, RSQLite reports the parameter position as a 0-indexed value rather than a 1-indexed value.

e.g. the following code has an error in the second params value, but error is reported as being in "Parameter 1".

``` r
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

sqlite_file <- 'test.db'
unlink(sqlite_file)
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), sqlite_file)

dbGetQuery(
    con, "CREATE TABLE records(x REAL, y REAL);"
)


# The following results in:
#   - Error: Parameter 1 does not have length 1.
#
dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "INSERT INTO records (x, y) VALUES (:x, :y)",
    params = list(x = 1, y = list(1,2))
)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

title: Loading table with NA values returns incorrect class
description:
I received an email about the new version of `RSQLite` to be released on August 5 potentially breaking my package. I have downloaded the development version, and think I found a bug. Loading a table with `NA` values causes the class of the columns with `NA` values to be changed to 'character.' Please see the example below:

```
library(RSQLite)
library(data.table)

## Create a connection to a new database
dbcon <- dbConnect(drv = SQLite(), db = "testdb.sqlite")

## Create a table, 'tb1'
status <- dbSendQuery(dbcon, "CREATE TABLE tb1 (val DOUBLE);")
status
dbClearResult(status)

## Add a data.table with NA values to 'tb1'
dat <- data.table(val = c(NA, 1:3, NA, 4:5))
dbWriteTable(dbcon, "tb1", dat, append = TRUE)

## Load all of 'tb1'
result <- DBI::dbGetQuery(dbcon, "SELECT * FROM tb1;")
dbDisconnect(dbcon)

## 'val' has the wrong class 
class(result$val)
# [1] "character"
```

In the current version on CRAN the class returns as 'numeric.'

title: dbSendPreparedQuery
description:
I believe the soft-deprecated (#153) dbSendPreparedQuery creates a confusing error message. "Named parameters not used in query".  It still works, but I do not understand what to use as the alternative params syntax with dbExecute. Note that I use it for Autoincrement with bulk inserts, which works ok when the field is NA in the data frame

```
# Parametrized queries
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

# Adapt dbname here
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = "C:/tmp/testparquery.sqlite")

if (!dbExistsTable(con, "PatientAuto")) {
  createAuto =
    'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS PatientAuto (
    PatientID INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT  NOT NULL ,
    Name TEXT
  )'

  createId =
    'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Patient (
    PatientID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL ,
    Name TEXT
  )'


  dbExecute(con, createAuto)
  dbExecute(con, createId)
} else {
  dbExecute(con, "DELETE from PatientAuto")
  dbExecute(con, "DELETE from Patient")
}

params = data.frame(PatientID = c(1,2), Name = c("Einstein", "Freud"))
paramsAuto = data.frame(PatientID = c(NA,NA), Name = c("Einstein", "Freud"))

# Warns about unused parameters, but works
# "Named parameters not used in query: PatientID, Name"
# This is "soft-deprecated
# https://github.com/rstats-db/RSQLite/issues/153
ret = dbSendPreparedQuery(con, "INSERT INTO  Patient VALUES(?,?)", bind.data = params)
dbClearResult(ret)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * from Patient")

# Using NA for Autoincrement parameters
# Warns about unused parameters, but works
ret = dbSendPreparedQuery(con, "INSERT INTO  PatientAuto VALUES(?,?)", bind.data = paramsAuto)
dbClearResult(ret)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * from PatientAuto")

# Cleanup
dbExecute(con, "DELETE from PatientAuto")
dbExecute(con, "DELETE from Patient")

# What is the suggested alternative? The versions below do not work
dbExecute(con,  "INSERT INTO  Patient VALUES(?,?)", params = params )
dbExecute(con,  "INSERT INTO  Patient VALUES(?,?)", params = list(PatientID = 1, Name = "Hallo") )

### Added after Kiril's suggestion (works!)
dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO PatientAuto VALUES($PatientID,$Name)", params = paramsAuto )

dbDisconnect(con)

```

Second, as far as I can tell, somewhere after `sqldf` calls `dbWriteTable(connection, nam2, DF, row.names = row.names)`, the data frame that is eventually passed to the SQL database then somehow gets an extra column, which is a copy of an existing column of the original data frame. I am happy to share the code and data to reproduce this but at the moment my data generating process is somewhat. Maybe I can distil this into a smaller data frame that is still failing.

title: left_join loses columns when using dplyr (reprex)
description:
left_join loses columns when using dplyr, reprex below.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library('dplyr'))

runJoinExperiment <- function(prefix, sc, eagerCompute) {
  names <- paste('t', prefix, 1:10, sep= '_')
  joined <- NULL
  for(ni in names) {
    di <- data.frame(x=1:3, y=1:3)
    if(!is.null(sc)) {
      ti <- copy_to(sc, di, ni)
    } else {
      ti <- di
    }
    if('NULL' %in% class(joined)) {
      joined <- ti
    } else {
      joined <- left_join(joined, ti, by= 'x')
      if(eagerCompute) {
        joined <- compute(joined)
      }
    }
  }
  compute(joined)
}

# works as expected
runJoinExperiment('inmem', NULL, FALSE)
```

title: Table not found
description: The new RSQLite seems to break sqldf, apparently. It says it can't find my tables. I looked this up and the sqldf package team has traced this issue back to the new RSQLite version.

title: problem with RSQLite 1.1-1 and sqldf
description:
On this page it was reported that there is a problem using sqldf with RSQLite after upgrading to RSQLite 1.1-1.   

  http://stackoverflow.com/questions/41511901/sqldf-create-table-from-data-frame-error-no-such-table-and-two-tables-crea 

I haven't looked into it but it was confirmed by the user that downgrading back to RSQLite 1.0.0 resolves the problem.  Please fix.

title: dbIsValid fails
description:
Not sure if this is RSQLite specific or a DBI issue, but I see it in RSQLite.

If I have a stale database connection `con` (e.g. left over from a previous R session), then `dbIsValid(con)` used to return `FALSE`, but since a recent update it signals an error, 

    > dbIsValid(con)
    Error in rsqlite_connection_valid(dbObj@ptr) : 
      external pointer is not valid

I can work around this, but shouldn't it just work?

To reproduce:

    library(RSQLite)
    con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), ":memory:")
    dbDisconnect(con)
    f <- tempfile()
    saveRDS(con, f)
    con <- readRDS(f)
    dbIsValid(con)

title: SpatiaLite extension
description: Is there any obvious way to deal with the SpatiaLite extension? In particular how can I **write** a SpatiaLite database with `RSQLite`?

title: Why backticks in `name`
description:
On recompiling old code, I got the message:

    Please use  `name` = "<savepoint>" to specify the name of the savepoint.

I there special meaning in the backticks?  Why not simply 

`name = "<savepoint>"`

title: dbExecute returns the last value when executing drop table
description:
According to the documentation, dbExecute() is supposed to return the "number of rows affected by the statement".  This tends to work, but it appears that when dropping a table dbExecute() instead returns the number of rows affected by the last call to dbExecute().  If no previous statements were executed then it returns 1 row affected independent of the number of rows in the table that was dropped.

```
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

data(USArrests)
dim(USArrests) # 50 rows

dbWriteTable(con, "USArrests", USArrests)

dbExecute(con, "delete from USArrests where UrbanPop < 50") # 8 rows deleted

dbExecute(con, "drop table USArrests") # 8 rows affected?

dbDisconnect(con)
```

This was on RSQlite v2.0.

title: Handling of 64bit integers
description:
I  just ran into an issue with RSQLite and 64bit integers from the bit64 package.

Here is a simplified example:
```R
library(DBI)
library(bit64)
dbcon = dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

df = data.frame(int64=as.integer64("12345678901234567"))

dbWriteTable(dbcon, "table", df)
dbReadTable(dbcon, "table")
#          int64
#1 7.749004e-308
```

A version with `dbBind` yields similar results:
```R
dbExecute(dbcon, "create table 'b' ('int64' INTEGER)")
dbres = dbSendStatement(dbcon, "insert into b(int64) values (?)")
dbBind(dbres, as.integer64(1))
dbGetRowsAffected(dbres)
dbClearResult(dbres)
dbGetQuery(dbcon, "select * from b")
#          int64
#1 4.940656e-324
```

A remedy is of course to `as.character` or `as.numeric` the offending values, but it would be nice if cases like these could be handled transparently.

 I ran into this when transferring data from one sqlite-db to another via R, where one column marked as integer had one very large value>2^32, thus making the whole column a bit64::integer64 column in R. If I hadn't been careful I wouldn't have noticed it immediately.

title: Doesn't work in parallel
description:
Below is a small program which simply uses two R process's to insert integers into a table. The table is created as "create table vals (value integer not null)". I created it outside the driver function simply to investigate whether it's an issue between the main the child process. It's not. After about 50 inserts, I get an error, which is not helpful since R loses the actual error when mcapply is used.

In any case, I tried starting and ending a transaction, as well as unloading the driver - same. Looks like the database gets locked and the other writes fail.

```
require(RSQLite)
require(parallel)

write.one.value = function(val, db.path)
{
   driver = SQLite()
   connection = dbConnect(driver, dbname=db.path)

   data = expand.grid(val)
   colnames(data) = c("value")
   query = paste("insert into vals (value) values (@value)", sep="")
   dbGetPreparedQuery(connection, query, bind.data=data)
   dbDisconnect(connection)
}

write.values = function(db.path)
{
   res = mclapply(seq(1,100,1), write.one.value, mc.cores=2, db.path=db.path)
}

# write.values("~/db.sqlite")
```
